q: How many players does each football team have on the pitch?
fact: Football's rules were first written down by the newly formed Football Association in London in 1863.

q: Legend says William Webb Ellis invented which sport by running with the ball in 1823?
fact: The trophy for the men's Rugby World Cup is called the Webb Ellis Cup in his honour.

q: The term 'hat-trick' was first used in which sport?
fact: In 1858 bowler H. H. Stephenson took three wickets in three balls in Sheffield, and fans bought him a hat.

q: In which sport might you perform a Salchow?
fact: The jump is named after Swedish skater Ulrich Salchow, who first landed it in competition in 1909.

q: At the first modern Olympics in 1896, what did event winners receive?
fact: Runners-up got a copper medal and a laurel branch, while third place received nothing at all.

q: Cluedo was invented in the 1940s by a musician from which English city?
fact: Waddingtons first published Cluedo in 1949, and in America it was renamed simply Clue.

q: How many holes are in a standard round of golf?
fact: The number was set in 1764, when St Andrews merged some short holes and cut its Old Course from 22 holes to 18.

q: In chess, which piece can only ever move diagonally?
fact: Because it only moves diagonally, a bishop stays on squares of the same colour for the whole game.

q: In tennis, what is a score of zero called?
fact: One popular theory says the 15, 30, 40 scoring came from quarter-hour marks on a clock face.

q: Which sport is played with a shuttlecock?
fact: The sport is named after Badminton House in Gloucestershire, the country seat of the Dukes of Beaufort.

q: In snooker, how many points is the black ball worth?
fact: A maximum break, potting all 15 reds with a black each followed by every colour, scores 147.

q: Cricket's Ashes series is contested between England and which country?
fact: The Ashes began with a mock obituary in 1882 declaring English cricket dead after a defeat at the Oval.

q: Which country hosted the first FIFA World Cup in 1930?
fact: The hosts also won it, beating Argentina 4–2 in the final in Montevideo.

q: What is the official distance of a marathon?
fact: The odd distance comes from the 1908 London Olympics, whose course ran from Windsor Castle to the stadium.

q: The Stanley Cup is the famous trophy of which sport?
fact: It is named after Lord Stanley of Preston, a Governor General of Canada, who donated it in 1892.

q: Which board game has squares marked 'triple word score'?
fact: Inventor Alfred Butts worked out how many of each letter to include partly by counting letters in newspapers.

q: How many interlocking rings are on the Olympic flag?
fact: Pierre de Coubertin designed the rings in 1913; with the white background, their colours covered every nation's flag.

q: What colour jersey does the overall leader wear in the Tour de France?
fact: Yellow was chosen because L'Auto, the newspaper that organised the first races, was printed on yellow paper.

q: Which is the most expensive property on the classic UK Monopoly board?
fact: Monopoly grew out of The Landlord's Game, which Elizabeth Magie patented in 1904.

q: In which sport do players slide stones across ice while teammates sweep?
fact: Many Olympic curling stones are carved from granite quarried on Ailsa Craig, a tiny island off Scotland.

q: Foil, épée and sabre are the three weapons of which sport?
fact: Fencing is one of only a handful of sports to have featured at every modern Olympic Games since 1896.

q: What do all the dots on a standard six-sided dice add up to?
fact: On a standard dice, the numbers on opposite faces always add up to seven.

q: Which martial art's name means 'empty hand'?
fact: Karate developed on the island of Okinawa, in what is now southern Japan.

q: Who was the first person to run a mile in under four minutes?
fact: He clocked 3 minutes 59.4 seconds at Iffley Road in Oxford on 6 May 1954.

q: In which event did athletes first see the 'Fosbury flop'?
fact: Dick Fosbury used his backwards technique to win Olympic gold at the 1968 Mexico City Games.

q: How many pieces does each player start with in draughts?
fact: Draughts is played only on the dark squares of the same 8×8 board used for chess.

q: The game Snakes and Ladders originated in which country?
fact: In the original Indian game, the ladders stood for virtues and the snakes for vices.

q: The ancient Olympic Games were held in honour of which Greek god?
fact: By tradition the first recorded Games, in 776 BC, had just one event: a sprint of about 190 metres.

q: In table tennis, a game is won by the first player to reach how many points?
fact: Games used to be played to 21 points until the rules were changed in 2001.

q: The fast stick-and-ball sport of hurling is native to which country?
fact: The women's version of hurling has its own name: camogie.

q: The Rubik's Cube was invented by an architecture lecturer from which country?
fact: A standard 3×3 cube can be arranged in more than 43 quintillion different ways.

q: Which sport did astronaut Alan Shepard play on the Moon in 1971?
fact: Shepard smuggled up a six-iron head and attached it to the handle of a tool for collecting lunar samples.

q: Volleyball was originally known by what name when it was invented in 1895?
fact: William G. Morgan invented it at a YMCA in Massachusetts as a gentler alternative to basketball.

q: The Calcutta Cup is contested by England and Scotland in which sport?
fact: The trophy was made from melted-down silver rupees left over when the Calcutta Football Club closed.

q: What is the name of the circular ring in which sumo wrestlers compete?
fact: Before a bout, sumo wrestlers throw a handful of salt into the ring to purify it.

q: Squash is said to have been invented around 1830 at which English school?
fact: Pupils noticed that a punctured ball 'squashed' on hitting the wall, which made for a more varied game.

q: Which card game uses a pegboard to keep score?
fact: Cribbage is credited to the English poet Sir John Suckling, who is said to have devised it in the early 17th century.

q: How long is a cricket pitch from stumps to stumps?
fact: 22 yards is exactly one chain, an old unit that land surveyors used for centuries.

q: Which sport was patented in 1874 under the name 'Sphairistikè'?
fact: Major Walter Wingfield sold his new game in boxed sets containing rackets, balls and a net.

q: The ancient board game Go is played on a grid of how many lines by how many?
fact: Go was invented in China more than 2,500 years ago, making it one of the oldest board games still played.
